title: Cost-Performance Optimization for Processing Low-Resource Language Tasks Using Commercial LLMs
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024
problem_statement: Commercial Large Language Model (LLM) cloud services charge users based on input and output token counts, creating severe economic and performance disadvantages for low-resource languages (LRLs). Because LLM tokenizers are optimized primarily for high-resource language (HRL) vocabularies, LRL words undergo severe subword over-fragmentation, multiplying token consumption by 2x to 7x per word compared to English. This tokenization disparity significantly increases API query costs while native LRL queries frequently suffer from inferior task accuracy.
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Commercial Large Language Model APIs, Low-Resource Languages (LRL), Indic Languages, Cost-Performance Optimization, Tokenization Disparity, Cross-Lingual Preprocessing
theoretical_framework: Subword tokenization disparity and over-fragmentation theory in multilingual language models (Petrov et al., 2023; Ahia et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2021); cross-lingual transfer via machine translation, transliteration, and code-mixing; prompt engineering strategies for multilingual reasoning; and the novel Relative Performance to Cost Ratio (RTPCR) optimization framework balancing task accuracy against token-based API expenditures.
methodology: The authors formulated the Relative Performance to Cost Ratio (RTPCR) metric to evaluate preprocessing strategies against native-script baseline querying across task performance and API token expenditure. They evaluated five client-side preprocessing techniques on input instances before passing them to commercial LLM APIs (GPT-4-0613): (1) Native script baseline, (2) Translation to English via open-source machine translation (IndicTrans2), (3) Explicit translation to English using GPT-4 API before task inference, (4) Implicit translation instructing GPT-4 to translate instances internally in the background if needed, (5) Wordmix (replacing excessively fragmented LRL words with English translations via dictionary lookup, as well as Wordmix(Hi) using Hindi and Word-to-Word W2W translation), and (6) Transliteration of LRL text into Latin script using Indic-Trans. The methodology was evaluated across 5 classification tasks from IndicXTREME and 6 generative tasks spanning 15 Indian languages (Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu, Urdu, Nepali, Kashmiri) plus Thai, Swahili, and Chinese, alongside fact-mutability probing on Indic-MULAN Wikidata triplets.
datasets: IndicXTREME: 5 classification datasets across 15 Indian languages (IndicSentiment for sentiment analysis, IndicXNLI for natural language inference, IndicCOPA for causal reasoning, IndicQA / IndicHeadline for topic and sentence classification)
XLSUM: Multilingual abstractive summarization corpus evaluated via ROUGE across low-resource languages
chaii (Hindi and Tamil Question Answering) and TyDi QA: Information-seeking question answering datasets evaluated via Exact Match (EM)
Samanantar: Large-scale parallel corpus for 11 Indic languages evaluated for Machine Translation via BLEU
Mathematical Reasoning Datasets: MGSM (Multilingual Grade School Math), Conic10K, and ArMath evaluated via Exact Match (EM)
Indic-MULAN: Curated Wikidata fact-verification dataset comprising <subject, relation, object> triplets across 11 Indian languages categorized into mutable, immutable-1, and immutable-n relations

metrics: Exact Match (EM for Question Answering and Mathematical Reasoning: chaii, TyDi QA, MGSM, Conic10K, ArMath)
Average tokens generated per instance (Cost proxy)
evaluation.evaluated_llm: OpenAI GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613 via API, temperature close to 0, seed=42)
evaluation.language_coverage: 15 Indian languages (Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu, Urdu, Nepali, Kashmiri) and 3 non-Indic languages (Thai, Swahili, Chinese)

key_findings: Commercial LLM tokenizers severely over-fragment low-resource Indic languages, generating 2x to 7x more tokens per word than English and imposing an unfair financial burden on LRL users.

Tokenization over-segmentation is significantly more severe for Dravidian languages (Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada) than for Indo-Aryan North Indian languages (Hindi, Bengali), reflecting disproportionate representation in LLM pretraining data.

Translating LRL inputs to English using an open-source MT system (IndicTrans2) is the optimal strategy, reducing GPT-4 API costs by up to ~90% while simultaneously boosting downstream classification accuracy and RTPCR across almost all tested languages.
Explicit translation using GPT-4 produces high task accuracy but incurs double API querying costs, resulting in the lowest overall RTPCR score among all tested methods.

Implicit background translation prompting improves performance on summarization, MT, and QA generation tasks without requiring auxiliary external MT tools or adding client-side token translation costs.
Transliterating LRL script into Latin script drastically lowers token counts and reduces API cost, but causes modest degradation in task performance due to grammatical and lexical ambiguities.

Wordmixing excessively segmented LRL words with English (Wordmix-En) or Hindi (Wordmix-Hi) dictionary equivalents maintains competitive task performance while cutting costs, demonstrating that syntax preservation is critical as full word-to-word (W2W) substitution degrades performance.

The proposed RTPCR metric effectively resolves limitations of the Parity Premium metric when task difficulty is language-independent, providing a superior guide for cost-performance trade-offs in commercial LLM deployment.
scope_and_delimitations: Commercial LLM evaluation is delimited to a single black-box model: OpenAI GPT-4 (specifically the gpt-4-0613 snapshot accessed via API under fixed seed=42 and near-zero temperature).
Primary linguistic focus is delimited to 15 scheduled and regional Indian languages, with supplementary evaluation on Thai, Swahili, and Chinese.
Task scope covers 5 classification tasks from IndicXTREME, 6 generation tasks (summarization, QA, MT, math reasoning), and fact-mutability probing via Indic-MULAN.
Hardware scope is delimited to a standard 16GB RAM CPU workstation for client-side preprocessing without local GPU acceleration.

Cost modeling is delimited to token-based cloud API pricing ($0.03/1K input tokens, $0.06/1K output tokens) and excludes operational infrastructure costs such as power, cooling, or local server deployment.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: Despite high costs, GPT-4 is widely regarded as providing better quality than open-source counterparts like BLOOM [\(Scao et al.,](#page-10-3) [2023\)](#page-10-3) and GPTneo. GPT-4 has been compared and shown to be superior to BARD in multiple application scenarios including text processing and understanding[<sup>3</sup>](#page-9-15) . For this reason, and to contain costs, we only experiment with one commercial LLM, GPT-4. Although it will increase the experiment cost significantly, bringing other paid LLMs into the experimental setup will make our observations more robust. Also, our wordmix technique, where we replace an LRL word with its translation, without taking sentence context into account, is crude it sometimes impacts sentence structure. Replacing a word or phrase while considering sentence context will be more appropriate. In this work, we only focus on Indian languages. Although we cover as many as 15 languages, an immediate extension can be to check the hypothesis for other LRLs worldwide.
limitations.summary: The authors acknowledge several explicit limitations: evaluation was restricted to a single commercial LLM (GPT-4) without comparing alternative commercial APIs such as Claude, Gemini, or BARD; the heuristic wordmix replacement strategy operates independently of sentence context, occasionally degrading syntactic integrity and semantic coherence; the empirical scope was primarily restricted to Indian languages rather than global low-resource languages; and translation-based approaches remain vulnerable to translation inaccuracies and subtle losses in sentiment nuance or cultural specificity.

generalizability_gap: The empirical investigation focuses primarily on 15 Indian languages, leaving low-resource indigenous languages from Africa, the Americas, and Southeast Asia largely unexamined. Furthermore, only GPT-4 was tested, so findings may vary across other commercial LLM families (such as Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, or proprietary mistral models) and newer tokenizer architectures.
methodological_gap: The wordmix algorithm performs context-independent, dictionary-based word replacement that does not consider syntactic dependencies or multi-word phrases; machine translation errors (e.g., loss of sarcasm, emotion, or cultural nuances) are directly propagated into downstream LLM inference; and the experimental framework assessed each preprocessing strategy in isolation without investigating hybrid cascades or dynamic routing based on tokenization entropy.
future_work: Extending the cost-performance optimization framework to a broader spectrum of commercial LLMs and multilingual foundation models beyond GPT-4.
Developing context-aware and phrase-level wordmixing heuristics to preserve syntactic structure and morphological agreement when mixing LRL and HRL vocabulary.
Exploring wordmixing with other high-resource regional bridge languages from the same language families rather than relying exclusively on English or Hindi.
Validating the preprocessing techniques and RTPCR framework across non-Indic low-resource language families globally.
Designing adaptive routing pipelines that dynamically select between native querying, open-source translation, transliteration, and wordmixing based on tokenization over-segmentation thresholds.
